name: Decaying turbulence
question: Why do two-dimensional eddies grow as the flow decays?

plots.title: Energy & enstrophy
plots.explain: Domain-averaged kinetic energy per unit mass and enstrophy (absolute, nondimensional units, L = 2π). Time integration is explicit RK4, so with ν = 0 energy is conserved to truncation error, not exactly. In decaying 2-D turbulence the energy is nearly conserved while enstrophy falls as small eddies merge (inverse cascade).

spec_decay.name: Decaying Turbulence
spec_decay.question: Why do two-dimensional eddies grow as the flow decays?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: Why do two-dimensional eddies grow as the flow decays?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: A random swirl of vorticity left to evolve. Like-signed vortices merge into larger ones — the 2-D inverse energy cascade — while enstrophy is dissipated at small scales.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Change the seed (advanced) for a different realisation.

layers.title: Physical explanation
layers.text:
Whenever two fluid layers slide past each other at different velocities, the shear layer between them is unstable: a small wavy perturbation on the interface speeds the flow over its crests and slows it in its troughs, and by Bernoulli's principle the resulting pressure differences amplify the wave. The wave then rolls over into a regular row of spiral vortices — the Kelvin–Helmholtz billows. Neighbouring billows pair up and merge, growing the layer and feeding a cascade toward two-dimensional turbulence.

You can see these billows directly in the wave-like 'KH cloud' formations in the sky, in the cloud bands of Jupiter, and in the mixing layers of the ocean, the atmosphere, jet engines and stellar winds. In two dimensions the turbulence is special: energy flows from small scales to large (the inverse cascade) while enstrophy flows down to small scales, the opposite of 3D turbulence.

This exhibit is solved with a pseudo-spectral method, which represents the flow as a sum of Fourier modes (sine/cosine waves). Derivatives become simple multiplications in Fourier space, so the method is extremely accurate — the gold standard for smooth, periodic turbulence problems.

layers.title: Equations, symbols and assumptions
layers.text:
• ω — the vorticity (the local spin of the fluid), the quantity being evolved
• u — velocity, recovered from the streamfunction ψ
• ∂t ω + (u·∇)ω — transport of vorticity by the flow
• ν∇²ω — viscous diffusion of vorticity
• ∇²ψ = −ω — the streamfunction ψ is obtained from vorticity by inverting the Laplacian (a simple division in Fourier space), then u = (∂ψ/∂y, −∂ψ/∂x)

layers.title: Initial and boundary conditions (this preset)
layers.ic: A random vorticity field with a peaked spectrum around wavenumber 14, drawn on a fixed 256² reference grid from the seed and truncated or zero-padded to the chosen resolution, so the same seed gives the same initial field at every resolution.

layers.title: Numerical method, checks and limitations
layers.text: A pseudo-spectral vorticity–streamfunction formulation on a periodic box: every spatial derivative is taken in Fourier space via the FFT, the nonlinear advection term is formed in physical space with 2/3-rule dealiasing, and time advances with classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta (stable for the advection operator's imaginary eigenvalues).

layers.title: References
items: Boffetta, G. & Ecke, R.E. (2012). Two-dimensional turbulence. Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech. 44, 427–451.

init.label: Initial field
init.help: Shear layers roll into Kelvin–Helmholtz billows; random turbulence decays as vortices merge (the 2-D inverse cascade); the Taylor–Green vortex is an exact decaying solution (energy ∝ exp(−4νt)) used to check the solver.

viscosity.label: Viscosity ν
viscosity.help: Kinematic viscosity ν — how 'thick' the fluid is. Lower → finer, more chaotic structures; higher → smoother, damped flow.

perturbation.label: Shear perturbation
perturbation.help: Amplitude of the initial transverse velocity kick that seeds the billows.

thickness.label: Shear-layer thickness
thickness.help: Thickness of each tanh shear layer as a fraction of the box size L.

seed.label: Random seed
seed.help: Seed of the random initial vorticity (same seed → same experiment).

resolution.label: Resolution
resolution.help: Grid resolution. It changes the grid, and with it whatever a scene ties to the grid: the elapsed convective time in the wind tunnel, the Rayleigh number in the convection scenes, the grain size in the rock, the extent of the blast box. The derived readouts say what moved for this experiment; runs at different resolutions are comparable only where they say so.

duration.label: Duration (×)
duration.help: Simulated interval as a multiple of the scene's reference interval (1.0 = default).
